Good morning. Imagine you point your phone at a painting in a museum, and a guide tells you its style. Our museum wants exactly this, on kiosks in its galleries. We worked on five styles: Baroque, Cubism, Impressionism, Pop Art and Ukiyo-e. The kiosks have small CPUs, the team is small and the budget is limited. So the director asks one question: is a neural network worth it in production, or would a simpler classical model do the job?

TRANSITION: To answer it, we did not jump straight to a model. So now, here is our path: six steps.

Step one: the data, and a fair test. Step two: our own neural network. Step three: we monitor its training and fix it. Step four: a pretrained ResNet18. Step five: a final test against a classical model. Step six: the cost on a kiosk. Each step told us what to try next. At the end of these six steps, we will have our answer.

TRANSITION: So now, let's start with step one: the data, and how we made the test fair.

We took 1 500 paintings from WikiArt, 300 per style. We cut them into three piles: 1 061 to train, 219 to validate, that is, to choose our settings, and 220 to test, used only once, at the very end. One rule matters a lot: all the paintings of a known painter go to the same pile. With a random split, 23 of our 32 known painters would be in two piles, and a model could learn to recognise Monet instead of Impressionism. With our split: zero. We measured it: when the model has seen the painter, it scores 11 points higher.

TRANSITION: We saw that our data is ready and our test is fair. So now, step two: we can build our first model.

Our first model is the simplest neural network of the course: a multi-layer perceptron built from nn.Linear layers and ReLU. It reads the pixels of a 64 by 64 image: 12 288 inputs and 6.4 million parameters. Before trusting it, we ran two checks. First, a model that knows nothing should have a loss of ln 5, about 1.61. Ours started at 1.99, too confident, so we made its last layer smaller and got 1.59. Second, it must be able to learn one small batch by heart: it does, 100 percent. Then the real training. The training accuracy goes to 99.7 percent, but the validation accuracy stays around 40 percent. This is overfitting: the network learns the paintings by heart.

TRANSITION: We saw that our MLP is overfitting. So now, step three: we try to fix this overfitting.

Before fixing it, we looked inside the network to check that the training itself was healthy: the gradient reaches every layer and only 4 percent of the neurons are dead. So the problem really is overfitting. Then we attacked the overfitting with the tools of session 6, 3 seeds each. All together, weight decay, dropout, batch norm, flips and early stopping take the MLP from 38.8 to 45.5 percent, and the gap between train and validation from 0.61 to 0.12. But one number shows a deeper limit: the MLP finds only 7 percent of the Cubist paintings. It sees colours, not shapes.

TRANSITION: We saw that the overfitting is under control. But our MLP still sees colours, not shapes. So now, step four: we need a network that sees shapes.

There is a type of network made for images, which recognises shapes: the convolutional network. We used ResNet18, the smallest ResNet. Its 18 layers slide small filters over the picture: the first layers find edges and colours, the next ones textures, the last ones shapes. Our MLP saw 12 288 separate pixels. ResNet18 already learned all this on 1.2 million ImageNet photos. We only have 1 061 paintings, so we keep it as it is: it is frozen. It turns each painting into 512 numbers. We train only the last layer, which turns these 512 numbers into our 5 styles: 2 565 weights. Like hiring an experienced art expert, and only teaching them our five style names.

TRANSITION: We saw how ResNet18 works. So now, let's see what it gives on our paintings.

Training this last layer takes less than a second, and gives 88.1 percent on validation, almost twice our best MLP. And it does see shapes: it finds 71 percent of the Cubist paintings, against 7 for our MLP. We also tried fine-tuning, letting its last block learn too: 8.4 million weights for 1 061 paintings. It overfits: 85.4 percent. We monitored it like the MLP: the gap between train and validation is only 0.09, against 0.61 for our first MLP.

TRANSITION: We saw that ResNet18 reaches 88 percent. But to answer the director, we also need a challenger without any neural network. So now, step five: we build this classical challenger, then we test every model.

A classical model cannot read raw pixels well. So we first describe each painting with 102 hand-made numbers: 82 for its colours, and 20 for the direction and strength of its brush strokes. Then a random forest: 500 decision trees. Each tree asks yes or no questions on these numbers, like "many dark colours?", until it names a style. Each one learns from a random draw of the paintings, so they make different mistakes. They vote, and the vote cancels the mistakes. Like every model, we chose its settings on validation: 63.5 percent.

TRANSITION: We saw how our challenger works. So now, the final test: every model, on 220 paintings never seen before.

We opened the 220 test paintings only once, for every model. The pretrained models are at the top, from 83 to 88 percent. The random forest reaches 67; our MLP 41. Is the gap real? A paired bootstrap on the same test paintings gives our model a lead of 16.4 points over the random forest, between 9 and 24 points: it is not luck. One honest note: the fine-tuned model is first here, but it was second on validation, and we keep the model chosen before the test.

TRANSITION: We saw that the pretrained network is the most accurate. But accuracy is only half of the director's question. So now, step six: what does it cost on a kiosk?

We timed one photo at a time, from the image to the answer. The ResNet needs 53 milliseconds on one CPU thread, 26 with four threads: faster than a blink. Even on a kiosk four times slower, it answers in a fifth of a second. The model file is 45 megabytes.

TRANSITION: We saw that it is accurate, fast and cheap. So now, we have everything we need to answer the director.

On the test, our own MLP reached 41 percent, the best classical model 67, and the frozen ResNet18 83. So, our answer to the director: yes, a neural network is worth it, but a pretrained one that we reuse. We recommend a frozen ResNet18 with a linear head. Why? It is accurate: one visitor in six gets a wrong style, against one in three. It is fast enough for a modest CPU, and cheap for a small team: one small layer, retrained in seconds. We do not recommend our MLP, a classical model alone, or fine-tuning for now. Before the launch, we must test real photos taken at the kiosks, add more styles, and measure the real hardware. Thank you. We are happy to take your questions.
